title: Ukrainian Vladyslav Heraskevych’s appeal denied in skeleton ‘helmet of memory’ case
content:
Vladyslav Heraskevych, the Ukrainian skeleton athlete disqualified from Olympic competition Thursday for his refusal to change his helmet honoring fellow athletes who have died during Russia’s invasion of his country, had his appeal denied by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) on Friday.

In dismissing Heraskevych’s case, a sole arbitrator for the CAS’s ad hoc division, set up to handle Olympic cases quickly, said that the guidelines governing athlete expression that both the International Bobsleigh & Skeleton Federation (IBSF) and the International Olympic Committee (IOC) say Heraskevych violated “provide a reasonable balance between athletes’ interests to express their views, and athletes’ interests to receive undivided attention for their sporting performance on the field of play.”

CAS announced the decision about two hours before the final two heats of the men’s skeleton competition at the Milan Cortina Games were scheduled to begin in Cortina d’Ampezzo, Italy.

Heraskevych missed the first two runs of the men’s skeleton competition Thursday after being pulled from the start list following an eligibility ruling by the IBSF. The IOC then withdrew his Olympic accreditation before later reinstating it.

Heraskevych filed an appeal later Thursday, asking to be reinstated immediately or to be allowed to perform supervised provisional runs until CAS ruled on the case.

Heraskevych’s “helmet of memory,” which he wore during training sessions earlier this week, has been the subject of one of the biggest controversies this week at the Olympics. The IOC said the helmet, covered with images of Ukrainian athletes who have died since Russia’s invasion, violates its rules on athlete expression during competition. The IOC gave him the option of wearing a black armband during his race and only displaying his helmet afterward, but he refused.

Heraskevych countered that the IOC’s rules on messaging are unclear and that he didn’t believe the helmet violated the rules.

The CAS arbitrator sided with the IOC, saying they “found these limitations reasonable and proportionate, considering the other opportunities for athletes to raise awareness (in mixed zones, in press conferences, on social networks, or in Mr Heraskevych’s case, wearing the helmet during four training runs).”

According to Article 50.2 of the Olympic Charter, “no kind of demonstration or political, religious or racial propaganda is permitted in any Olympic sites, venues or other areas.” IOC spokesperson Mark Adams, though, said Thursday it was not the so-called “Rule 50” that was at issue, but rather Rule 40, which says athletes “shall enjoy freedom of expression” that is “in accordance with the Guidelines determined by the IOC executive board.”

“In Ukraine, we have a lot of tears, and I don’t want to doubt her feelings,” Heraskevych told reporters of his Thursday morning meeting with IOC president Kirsty Coventry, who was emotional after Heraskevych’s disqualification. “But I don’t believe we violated the rules.”

Coventry spoke Thursday about the rules existing to protect athletes from anyone pressuring them to represent ideas they’re uncomfortable with, and she reiterated that stance Friday.

“The rules are the rules, and I believe in the rules,” Coventry said in a Friday morning news conference. “The rules are the safest and fairest way for athletes to express themself and be kept safe.”

She added, “I don’t think it’s ever really been a question around (Heraskevych’s) messaging. It was where his messaging was happening.”
